analysis.one_liner: Counts GI Bill benefits toward for-profit colleges' federal-aid funding limit.
analysis.headline: A bill to stop for-profit colleges from using veterans' education benefits to dodge federal aid limits died in House subcommittees with no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law says for-profit colleges must get at least 10% of their revenue from somewhere other than federal student aid, or they lose that aid. The current rule doesn't count GI Bill and other veterans' education benefits as federal aid, so schools can enroll veterans to meet the 10% test while veterans' federal benefits keep flowing in. This bill would count veterans' benefits toward the limit and cut colleges off from Pentagon and VA education programs if they fail it.
analysis.who_benefits: Veterans and service members who attend for-profit colleges. If a school fails the stricter test, it loses federal student aid, Pentagon tuition assistance, and GI Bill eligibility, so schools would have to rely less on the veterans' benefits they currently use to stay compliant. Veterans' education benefits would be worth what they are supposed to be worth — funding a real education, not propping up a school's revenue math.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Veterans and service members using education benefits

how_it_helps.text: Renames the rule the 90/10-plus rule: a for-profit college must get at least 10% of its revenue from sources other than both federal student aid and veterans' education benefits, or lose federal student aid eligibility.

Requires the Education Department to notify the Defense and Veterans Affairs Departments whenever a college fails the test, and orders those departments to block their own education assistance from going to that college until it regains eligibility — so failing one program shuts down all three.

Defines veterans' education benefits broadly to cover every listed GI Bill-style program plus any other education assistance paid by the Defense or Veterans Affairs departments, closing off rebranding workarounds.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit college companies, whose business models depend heavily on federal dollars. Schools that currently stay compliant by counting veterans' benefits as non-federal revenue would have to find genuinely private revenue, cut enrollment, or fail the test and lose all federal education funding.

drawbacks.text: Because the bill makes a failing school ineligible for Pentagon and VA education programs, a school that loses eligibility could respond by limiting or discouraging veteran enrollment rather than by shrinking its reliance on federal money, which could reduce education options for some veterans.

The change takes effect July 1, 2016 with no phase-in, so schools operating near the 10% line would face a sudden funding cliff that could push marginal colleges into closure, leaving enrolled students mid-program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is a straightforward closing of a funding loophole: veterans' benefits count the same way other federal aid counts. The real cost falls on for-profit college companies that relied on veterans' enrollment for compliance, and the main risk to veterans is that schools might react by turning veterans away instead of restructuring. That risk is real but addressable through enforcement; on balance the bill protects the integrity of veterans' education benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and three subcommittees in late 2015, and none of them ever took it up; the Congress ended in January 2017 with no markup, no floor vote, no vote in the Senate. The bill was referred to the Education and the Workforce, Armed Services, and Veterans' Affairs Committees, then to subcommittees on Military Personnel, Economic Opportunity, and Higher Education and Workforce Training, and nothing further happened.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the bill on November 17, 2015 with two Democratic cosponsors, Reps. Conyers and Honda.
The Speaker referred it to three committees — Education and the Workforce, Armed Services, and Veterans' Affairs — a multi-referral that splits the bill among committees with different jurisdictions.
Within three weeks it was parceled out to three separate subcommittees: Military Personnel, Economic Opportunity, and Higher Education and Workforce Training.
The last recorded action in the 114th Congress is the March 23, 2016 subcommittee referral; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit college companies kept the current rule, under which veterans' GI Bill dollars count as non-federal revenue. Veterans attending those schools continued carrying the compliance burden.

for.name: Reps. John Conyers and Michael Honda

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after the November 2015 referral; no markup or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill's last recorded action in the Congress was a subcommittee referral on March 23, 2016.

against.name: House Armed Services and Veterans' Affairs Committees
against.what_they_did: Held the bill's Defense and VA provisions in subcommittee with no recorded action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed 90/10 changes that would count veterans' benefits as federal revenue, since the current rule lets schools use GI Bill enrollment to satisfy the federal-aid limit.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run committees that received the bill took no action.

industries.note: These schools currently operate under a rule requiring at least 10% of revenue from non-federal sources, but veterans' education benefits do not count as federal revenue under that rule, so veteran enrollment can keep a school compliant while its federal dependence stays high. The bill would count those benefits as federal revenue and cut schools that fail from federal student aid, Pentagon tuition assistance, and GI Bill programs. It matters for ordinary people because veterans' education benefits are a public commitment to those who served, and the bill would stop them from functioning as a compliance crutch for colleges that depend on federal money.

industries.industry: Veterans and military education-benefit programs (DoD tuition assistance and VA education benefits)
industries.note: The bill does not change what benefits veterans receive; it changes how colleges may count them, and adds a mechanism so that a school failing the funding rule is cut off from Defense and VA education programs as well as federal student aid.
